title: Periodic trend and periodicity: atomic radii, ionic radii, ionization energy, electron affinity, electronegativity, metallic characters (general trend and explanation only)
topicTitle: Periodic trend and periodicity: atomic radii, ionic radii, ionization energy, electron affinity, electronegativity, metallic characters (general trend and explanation only)
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — One Contest, Six Trends

Atomic radius, ionic radius, ionisation energy, electron affinity, electronegativity and metallic character are not six facts to memorise — they are **six readings of one contest**: effective nuclear charge (Z_eff) pulling electrons in versus shells and shielding pushing them out. Learn the contest and each trend's period/group direction — and the famous irregularities NEB 2022 asked — follow as derivations.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Atomic radius

- **Definition problem:** an electron cloud has no edge, so radius is defined operationally:
  - **Covalent radius:** half the internuclear distance between two bonded identical atoms (Cl–Cl → 99 pm).
  - **van der Waals radius:** half the closest distance between non-bonded atoms (larger than covalent).
  - **Metallic radius:** half the nearest-neighbour distance in a metal lattice.
- **Across a period:** Z_eff rises, same shell pulled in → **radius decreases** (Li 152 pm → F 71 pm; Na 186 → Cl 99). Noble gases (van der Waals radii) break the run.
- **Down a group:** a new shell opens, n grows → **radius increases** (Li 152 → Na 186 → K 231 pm).

### 2.2 Ionic radius

- **Cation < parent atom:** losing the outer shell and raising Z_eff per remaining electron (Na 186 pm → Na⁺ 95 pm).
- **Anion > parent atom:** added electrons increase repulsion, Z_eff per electron drops (Cl 99 pm → Cl⁻ 181 pm).
- **Isoelectronic series** (same electron count): radius **falls as Z rises** — N³⁻ > O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺ (all 10 e⁻).

### 2.3 Ionisation energy (IE / ionisation enthalpy)

- **IE₁:** energy to remove the most loosely bound electron from an isolated gaseous atom: M(g) → M⁺(g) + e⁻.
- **Across a period:** Z_eff ↑ → **IE increases** (Na 496 → Ar 1520 kJ mol⁻¹), with dips at Be→B and N→O.
- **Down a group:** n ↑, shielding ↑ → **IE decreases** (Li 520 → Cs 376).
- **Successive IEs always rise:** IE₁ < IE₂ < IE₃ — and a **huge jump** when the shell is emptied (Na: IE₂ ≫ IE₁, proving Na⁺ = [Ne]).

### 2.4 Electron affinity (EA) and electronegativity (EN)

- **EA:** energy released when an isolated gaseous atom gains an electron: Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g), −349 kJ mol⁻¹. Across a period EA generally **increases** (more negative); down a group it **decreases**. Nobel-gas EAs are positive (no tendency to gain).
- **EN:** the *tendency* of a bonded atom to attract the shared electron pair (Pauling scale, F = 4.0 highest). Same directions as EA but a property of **bonded** atoms, unitless.
- **EA vs EN:** EA is energy (measured, isolated atom); EN is relative tendency (scaled, bonded atom).

### 2.5 Metallic character

- Ease of losing electrons. **Across a period: decreases** (Na strongly metallic → Cl non-metallic); **down a group: increases** (Li → Cs, Cs is the most reactive metal). Metalloids line the B–Si–Ge–As–Sb–Te staircase.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Value to quote |
|---|---|---|
| **Covalent radius** | Half the distance between nuclei of two bonded identical atoms | Cl: 99 pm |
| **Ionisation energy** | Minimum energy to remove the outermost electron from isolated gaseous atom | Na IE₁ = 496 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| **Electron affinity** | Energy released on adding an electron to a neutral gaseous atom | Cl = −349 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| **Electronegativity** | Tendency of a bonded atom to attract the shared pair (Pauling) | F = 4.0, Cs = 0.7 |
| **Isoelectronic ions** | Ions with the same electron count, different Z | O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺ |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 NEB 2022 (3m, verified PYQ) — the two irregularities

**(a) IE₁(Mg) > IE₁(Al) although Mg lies left of Al.**
Mg: [Ne] 3s²; Al: [Ne] 3s² 3p¹. Mg's first electron comes from a **completely filled, stable 3s²** subshell; Al's comes from the higher-energy, shielded **3p** electron, which is easier to remove. Values: Mg 738 vs Al 578 kJ mol⁻¹. The Be→B dip has the same cause (2s² vs 2p¹).

**(b) Atomic radius of Na is greater than that of Cl.**
Na: [Ne] 3s¹, Z_eff ≈ +1; Cl: [Ne] 3s² 3p⁵, Z_eff ≈ +7. Same shell (n = 3), but Cl's far stronger net pull drags it inward: Na 186 pm vs Cl 99 pm. Radius is set by **Z_eff**, not by the electron count.

### 4.2 The other two standard dips (complete the picture)

- **Be → B:** B's 2p¹ electron is higher in energy and better shielded than Be's 2s² pair → IE falls.
- **N → O:** N is 2p³ (half-filled, exchange-stabilised); O's fourth p electron must **pair** and suffers repulsion → IE falls.
- **Group 18 anomaly in EA:** noble gases **refuse** electrons (filled shells), so their EA is positive (energy must be supplied) — the extreme end of the trend.

### 4.3 Successive ionisation energies read the configuration

Na (1s²2s²2p⁶3s¹): IE₁ = 496, IE₂ = 4562, IE₃ = 6912 kJ mol⁻¹ — the **9× jump** at IE₂ marks the crossing from the 3rd shell into the neon core. Magnesium's jump comes at IE₃. This is how IE data *prove* shell structure — a favourite application question.

### 4.4 The trend table (memorise directions, derive reasons)

| Property | Across a period (→) | Down a group (↓) | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Atomic radius | **Decreases** | **Increases** | Z_eff ↑ vs new shell |
| IE | **Increases** (dips Be→B, N→O) | **Decreases** | Z_eff ↑ vs shielding ↑ |
| EA | **Increases** (more negative) | **Decreases** | Z_eff ↑ vs size ↑ |
| EN | **Increases** | **Decreases** | Pull on shared pair |
| Metallic character | **Decreases** | **Increases** | Ease of losing e⁻ |
| Ionic size: cation | — | — | cation < atom; anion > atom |

**Periodic trends — across a period / down a group**

| Property | Across a period | Down a group | Famous exception |
|---|---|---|---|
| Atomic radius | Decreases | Increases | noble-gas radii (van der Waals) larger |
| Ionisation energy | Increases | Decreases | Be→B and N→O dips |
| Electron affinity | Increases (overall) | Decreases | F < Cl |
| Electronegativity | Increases | Decreases | — |
| Metallic character | Decreases | Increases | — |
| Oxide character | Basic → acidic | More basic down | Al₂O₃ amphoteric |

## 5. Comparison Tables

**IE vs EA vs EN**

| Basis | Ionisation energy | Electron affinity | Electronegativity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Process | Losing an electron | Gaining an electron | Attracting shared pair in a bond |
| Atom state | Isolated gaseous | Isolated gaseous | **Bonded** atom |
| Quantity | Energy absorbed (kJ mol⁻¹) | Energy released (kJ mol⁻¹) | Relative scale (unitless) |
| Period direction | Increases | Increases | Increases |
| Group direction | Decreases | Decreases | Decreases |
| Extremes | He highest; Cs lowest | Cl most negative | F = 4.0; Cs = 0.7 |

**Similarity:** all three measure electron-holding power; all rise with Z_eff across a period and fall down a group.

**Cation vs anion formation**

| Basis | Cation | Anion |
|---|---|---|
| Electrons | Lost | Gained |
| Size vs atom | **Smaller** | **Larger** |
| Z_eff per electron | Higher | Lower |
| Example | Na⁺ 95 pm (from 186) | Cl⁻ 181 pm (from 99) |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Radius dip exceptions:** noble-gas radii are **van der Waals** radii — larger than the neighbouring halogen's covalent radius; do not read them as a trend break in bonding radius.
**IE dips are about subshell stability:** Be→B is s² vs p¹ (energy level); N→O is half-filled vs paired (repulsion). Two different causes — quote the right one for the right pair.
**EA vs EN:** EA is measurable energy for an **isolated** atom; EN is a relative tendency of a **bonded** atom. Cl has the most negative EA but **F** has the highest EN.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (2m): Why is IE₂ of sodium enormously higher than IE₁?** — After IE₁, Na⁺ is [Ne] (1s²2s²2p⁶); IE₂ must remove an electron from the **filled inner shell** against a much higher Z_eff — 4562 vs 496 kJ mol⁻¹. The jump proves the 3s electron was the only valence electron.

**NEB-style (2m): Arrange O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺ in decreasing size and justify.** — All are 10-electron (isoelectronic); radius falls as nuclear charge rises: **O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺** (Z = 8, 9, 11, 12, 13 pulling the same cloud).

**NEB-style (2m): Why is Cs the most reactive metal and F the most reactive non-metal?** — Cs: largest alkali metal, lowest IE (376 kJ mol⁻¹) — loses its electron most easily. F: smallest halogen, highest EN (4.0) and very negative EA — gains an electron most avidly. The two extremes meet in CsF, the most ionic of fluorides.

**NEB-style (3m): How do atomic radii vary across a period and down a group? Give one reason for each.** — **Across a period:** radius decreases (Li 152 → F 71 pm; Na 186 → Cl 99 pm) — electrons enter the same shell while Z_eff rises, pulling the shell inward. **Down a group:** radius increases (Li 152 → Na 186 → K 231 pm) — each element adds a new principal shell, and shielding keeps Z_eff on the valence shell nearly constant, so the extra n dominates.

**NEB-style (2m): Define ionisation energy and explain why IE₁ < IE₂ < IE₃.** — IE₁ is the minimum energy to remove the most loosely bound electron from an isolated gaseous atom. Each successive removal pulls a more tightly held electron from an **increasingly positive ion** (higher Z_eff per electron), so IE₁ < IE₂ < IE₃, with a sharp jump at a core-shell crossing.

**NEB-style (2m): Distinguish electron affinity from electronegativity.** — **EA:** energy released when an **isolated gaseous atom** gains an electron (Cl: −349 kJ mol⁻¹) — a measurable thermodynamic quantity. **EN:** the relative tendency of a **bonded** atom to attract the shared electron pair (Pauling scale, F = 4.0) — a unitless comparative index. Both rise across and fall down the table, but they are not the same quantity.

**NEB-style (3m): How do atomic radii vary across a period and down a group? Give one reason for each.** — **Across a period:** radius decreases (Li 152 → F 71 pm; Na 186 → Cl 99 pm) — electrons enter the same shell while Z_eff rises, pulling the shell inward. **Down a group:** radius increases (Li 152 → Na 186 → K 231 pm) — each element adds a new principal shell, and shielding keeps Z_eff on the valence shell nearly constant, so the extra n dominates.

**NEB-style (2m): Define ionisation energy and explain why IE₁ < IE₂ < IE₃.** — IE₁ is the minimum energy to remove the most loosely bound electron from an isolated gaseous atom. Each successive removal pulls a more tightly held electron from an **increasingly positive ion** (higher Z_eff per electron), so IE₁ < IE₂ < IE₃, with a sharp jump at a core-shell crossing.

**NEB-style (2m): Distinguish electron affinity from electronegativity.** — **EA:** energy released when an **isolated gaseous atom** gains an electron (Cl: −349 kJ mol⁻¹) — a measurable thermodynamic quantity. **EN:** the relative tendency of a **bonded** atom to attract the shared electron pair (Pauling scale, F = 4.0) — a unitless comparative index. Both rise across and fall down the table, but they are not the same quantity.

confusion: **IE dips vs steady rise:** the period trend is "increases with two dips" — Be→B and N→O. A flat "increases" answer misses the marks reserved for the irregularities.
**Cation shrinkage is not just electron loss:** losing the whole outer shell (Na⁺) dominates; but even same-shell loss (Fe³⁺ vs Fe²⁺) shrinks the ion because Z_eff per electron rises.
importantConcepts: **Irregularities are the exam:** Mg > Al (3s² filled vs 3p¹) and Na > Cl radius (Z_eff on the same shell) — NEB 2022's pair; add Be→B and N→O for the complete IE picture.
examples: ***Na IE₁ = 496 → IE₂ = 4562 kJ mol⁻¹*** — a 9× jump: the second electron comes from the neon core. Successive-IE jumps are how shell structure was proven.
universalFacts: Francium is often cited as the most metallic element, but Cs is the *practically* most reactive metal — Fr is so radioactive (half-life 22 minutes) that bulk chemistry is unobservable.
importantStatements: "Atomic radius decreases across a period because the increasing effective nuclear charge pulls the same shell inward."
importantNotes: Verified PYQ: NEB 2022 3m — explain IE₁(Mg) > IE₁(Al) and r(Na) > r(Cl) (solved above). Other items are NEB-style practice.
examNotes: For irregularity questions, always write both configurations first (Mg 3s², Al 3s²3p¹) — the subshell contrast is the mark-earner; the numbers (738 vs 578) are garnish.
formulas:
- Z_eff = Z − σ (drives every trend)
- M(g) → M⁺(g) + e⁻, IE₁; IE₁ < IE₂ < IE₃
- Isoelectronic radius ∝ 1/Z (approx)
- Pauling EN: F 4.0 > O 3.5 > N 3.0 > Cl 3.0 … Cs 0.7
summary: Six trends, one contest. Across a period Z_eff climbs (same-shell shielding is poor): **radii shrink** (Na 186 → Cl 99 pm), **ionisation energy climbs** with two dips — Be→B (2s² vs 2p¹) and N→O (half-filled vs pairing) — **electron affinity and electronegativity rise** (Cl most negative EA, F highest EN), and **metallic character falls**. Down a group each new shell wins the contest: radii grow, IE falls, metals get more reactive (Cs the practical extreme). Ionic sizes obey Z_eff per electron: cations shrink below their atoms (Na⁺ 95 pm), anions swell above theirs (Cl⁻ 181 pm), and isoelectronic ions shrink as Z rises (O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺). NEB 2022's irregularities — Mg > Al in IE and Na > Cl in radius — are not exceptions to the trends but their sharpest demonstrations: subshell stability and Z_eff decide everything.

Increases down a group as new shells are added
Measured as covalent, metallic or van der Waals radius depending on the element

points: Cations are smaller than the parent atom; anions are larger
Isoelectronic series: radius falls as nuclear charge rises (Na+ < F- < O2-)
Higher charge on the same ion means smaller radius (Fe3+ < Fe2+)

subtopics.name: Ionisation energy
points: Energy to remove the most loosely bound electron from a gaseous atom
Increases across a period, decreases down a group
Successive ionisation energies always increase; large jumps reveal shell structure

subtopics.name: Electron affinity and electronegativity
points: Electron affinity is the energy change on adding an electron; more negative across a period
Electronegativity is the tendency to attract a shared pair; Pauling scale
Both increase across a period and decrease down a group

subtopics.name: Metallic character
points: Decreases across a period, increases down a group
Metals lose electrons readily; non-metals gain them
Metalloids show intermediate behaviour

points: IE of Be > B and N > O because of filled and half-filled subshell stability
IE of Mg > Al and P > S for the same reason
Electron affinity of F is less negative than Cl because of small size and electron repulsion

Subshell stability explains the exceptions
